rationale: A wins because it separates three real reporter shapes instead of stuffing the same store news into multiple envelopes. Its best line, "A canned-water brand says it has given $4.2M to clean-water charities. Here's what that buys," gives a reporter a checkable number, a skeptical frame, and the proof burden. B has decent bones, but "Liquid Death's first store sells T-shirts, limited-run cans and event tickets" invents specifics and turns the second store angle into a dressed-up sibling of the first.
gaps_in_A: "Liquid Death opens a store that sells almost no water" overstates the supplied facts. The update says merch, limited-edition canned water, and events; it does not give the water-versus-merch mix.
"The standard just got a stress test" is a strong frame, but it leans on an inferred B Corp controversy before proving there is one.

"the prevailing belief is that packaged single-serve water is the category sustainability certification exists to discourage" is too sweeping unless a reporter can back it with critics, standards experts, or prior coverage.
gaps_in_B: "T-shirts" and "event tickets" are invented. The update says merch and in-store events, not apparel categories or paid ticketing.
The first two store angles are too close: "what does owned retail do" and "what kind of company this is" both orbit the same flagship-as-marketing-asset story.

"Liquid Death certifies as a B Corp and says it has given $4.2M" collapses two better angles into one softer impact bundle. A reporter needs either the donation accounting story or the B Corp standards story, not a company virtue stack.
"brands that run merch and events as a business line" goes beyond the update. No facts establish merch/events as a business line rather than store programming.
